Field surveys of Twohorn sculpin in the Barents Sea have provided detailed morphometric data for this cold-water cottid. Females attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of 5.0 centimeters [Lp = 5.0 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 1.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.3 grams]. Comparative analysis with other members of the genus Icelus indicates that this length at maturation is relatively small, likely an adaptation to the consistently low temperatures and limited food resources of the Arctic benthos. The largest individuals recorded in the study population reached an ultimate total length of 12.8 centimeters [Li = 12.8 centimeters], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 26.4 grams [Wwi = 26.4 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from the same dataset. This asymptotic size suggests a modest growth trajectory, with most somatic expansion occurring prior to the onset of reproductive allocation.

Embryonic and larval development in Icelus bicornis proceeds slowly under near-freezing conditions, a common pattern among polar marine teleosts. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C] require approximately 113 days [ab = approximately 113 days] to complete development and hatch. This protracted incubation period is consistent with the reduced metabolic rates imposed by the cold thermal environment and the relatively small initial yolk reserves. At the moment of eclosion, the prolarvae possess a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a mass derived from the egg diameter of approximately 2 millimeters and reflecting a high yolk-to-embryo conversion efficiency. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after the completion of yolk-sac resorption, a critical period that defines the early life history of this benthic species.

Reproductive output in the Twohorn sculpin is constrained by the short, cold growing season typical of high-latitude seas. Under the same thermal regime of 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C], females produce a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year], with each spawning yielding an average of 725 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 725 eggs per clutch]. This exceptionally high fecundity is balanced by the large size of the individual eggs, which enhances larval survival through an extended yolk-dependent phase. The resulting annual reproductive rate is modest compared to temperate sculpins, but consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity in a stable but resource-poor environment.

Post-hatching development and maturation in Icelus bicornis unfold over a considerable span of time at Arctic temperatures. The time since birth at puberty for females is 730 days [tp = 730 days] when maintained at 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C], indicating that nearly two years of growth and physiological preparation are required before gonadal recrudescence is initiated. This prolonged juvenile period is characteristic of high-latitude fishes and is thought to reflect the energetic demands of achieving a threshold body size in a region where seasonal productivity pulses are brief. The onset of vitellogenesis during the second winter likely aligns with the period of maximal lipid storage from the previous summer's feeding, ensuring that sufficient reserves are available for gamete production.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the Twohorn sculpin under natural conditions is 4015 days [am = 4015 days] at 0.2 °C [T = 0.2 °C]. This substantial longevity is a common feature of slow-growing, cold-adapted species and allows for multiple reproductive events over a lifetime, even when annual fecundity is minimal. Senescence in this species is marked by a gradual decline in body condition and a reduction in reproductive activity during the final years of life. The extended lifespan, combined with the late age at maturity and low reproductive rate, places Icelus bicornis firmly at the slow end of the life-history continuum among Arctic cottids, a strategy well-suited to the stable but energy-limited ecosystems it inhabits.
